title: Ultrasonic Testing for Mining | UT Inspection (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for US mines and plants: haul truck frames, shafts, mill shells, conveyor pulleys, crusher parts. Send drawings for a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Mining and Minerals Processing in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT performs on-site ultrasonic testing (UT) for US mines, quarries and mineral processing plants: wall thickness surveys on mill shells, chutes and pipework, crack detection in shafts and pins, and weld examination on truck frames, booms and conveyor structures. Technicians are mobilized to the mine for the agreed scope. Send the component list and site details and request a UT inspection quote.

What ultrasonic testing is used for at a mine

A mine runs equipment that is large, loaded cyclically and worn continuously. Two things go wrong with it: material disappears (abrasion and corrosion thin steel from the inside), and cracks start where stress is highest and grow a little with every haul cycle or every swing of a boom. Ultrasonic testing answers both questions from one side of the part. A transducer sends sound into the steel, and the instrument reads the time and strength of the echoes that return. Thickness comes from the time to the back wall. A crack, lamination or lack of fusion shows up as an echo that arrives sooner than the back wall or from the wrong direction.

That matters on mining equipment because much of it cannot be dismantled for inspection. You cannot put a mill shell on a bench. UT lets a technician measure a trunnion, a mill shell weld or a boom chord while it stays where it is, and it can see below the surface where magnetic particle and penetrant testing stop. For surface cracks that are open to view, the sibling pages on magnetic particle inspection for mining and penetrant testing for mining are usually the faster tools, and we say plainly in the section further down when UT is the wrong choice.

Equipment and components we examine

The scope list below is typical of what mine maintenance planners ask us to quote. Each line is a separate examination with its own procedure and acceptance basis.

  • Haul truck frames and axle housings. Weld toes and box-section corners at the main rails, hoist cylinder mounts, suspension mounts and body pivots. Fatigue cracks start at these welds on trucks that run every shift.
  • Shovel and dragline booms. Chord and lacing welds, boom foot pins, boom point sheave pins, and dipper handle attachments. These are long, heavily welded structures where one crack can travel a long way before it is seen.
  • Crusher main shafts and eccentrics. Gyratory and cone crusher shafts carry large bending and impact loads. Straight-beam scanning from the end face looks for transverse fatigue cracks in the shaft body.
  • Mill trunnions, shells and girth gear mounts. Grinding mill shells and heads are welded plate, and the trunnion and shell flange area is a known place for cracking. Shell thickness also reduces under liners where wear and corrosion work together.
  • Conveyor pulleys, shafts and structures. Head and tail pulley shafts crack at keyways, hub fits and shaft shoulders. Gallery frames and transfer towers need thickness and weld checks where corrosion has taken hold.
  • Chutes, hoppers, slurry and tailings pipe. Thickness surveys on wear-prone elbows, impact plates and cyclone feed lines to find the thin areas before a hole forms.

Where we mobilize in mining country

Mines are far from major airports, so our crews are mobilized to the site rather than dispatched from a nearby base. Atlantis has no office near the site; planning therefore starts with the site address, the access rules and the dates of the shutdown window. These city pages explain the work for the mining regions we travel to.

  • Ultrasonic testing in Tucson is the usual entry point for the Arizona copper belt, with open pits, concentrators and leach operations within reach.
  • Ultrasonic testing in Phoenix covers central and eastern Arizona mines and the fabrication shops that rebuild their equipment.
  • Ultrasonic testing in Salt Lake City serves Utah copper and the Intermountain West, where large trucks and shovels work at altitude.
  • Ultrasonic testing in Minneapolis is the staging point for the Minnesota iron range and its taconite plants, with winter conditions to plan around.
  • Ultrasonic testing in Birmingham reaches Alabama coal and the steel and foundry supply chain around it.
  • Ultrasonic testing in Anchorage supports Alaska gold, zinc and gravel operations, where logistics and weather set the schedule.
  • Ultrasonic testing in Spokane is the base city for Inland Northwest and northern Rockies metals mining.
  • Ultrasonic testing in El Paso and Albuquerque cover New Mexico, west Texas and the southwestern copper and potash districts.

Codes, regulators and who decides acceptance

The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) regulates the work at the mine. Its rules sit in 30 CFR Parts 56 and 57 for surface and underground metal and nonmetal mines, and Parts 75 and 77 for underground and surface coal. Those parts require equipment to be maintained in safe condition and defects affecting safety to be corrected; they do not write an ultrasonic procedure. The procedure comes from industry standards and the equipment maker.

For the examination itself we work to ASME Section V, Article 4 for weld examination and Article 5 for thickness, to ASTM E797 for manual pulse-echo thickness measurement, ASTM E164 for contact examination of weldments, and ASTM E114 for straight-beam contact testing of shafts and forgings. The weld acceptance basis is normally AWS D1.1 for structural steel or AWS D14.3, the specification for welding earthmoving, construction and agricultural equipment, which suits truck bodies and frames. The owner or the equipment manufacturer chooses the criteria. Our report states which one was used and compares each indication against it; the decision to repair, monitor or retire the part stays with you or your engineer. Our technicians are qualified under Atlantis's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians perform and interpret the examination and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Explanatory guides are at ASME Section V Article 4 explained and Article 5 thickness requirements.

Technique details that matter on mining steel

Mining steel is not clean laboratory plate. Surfaces are pitted, painted, packed with fines or coated with rubber, and heavy sections attenuate sound. Our approach adjusts for that.

  • Surface preparation. Loose scale, paint and ore dust come off where the transducer sits. On a corroded shell we grind a clean footprint and record where it is, so repeat surveys read the same spot.
  • Couplant. Gel for ordinary conditions, heavier grades for rough or vertical faces, and a low-temperature couplant when the site is cold enough for a gel to stiffen. High-altitude Arizona and Utah mornings and Minnesota winters are both cold enough to matter.
  • Calibration. The instrument is calibrated on a reference block of similar material and velocity, and checked again at the end of the shift. On weld work the angle-beam probe is checked for exit point and beam angle on a calibration block before scanning.
  • Coverage. Shaft scans run from the end face and from the diameter at several positions so that cracks at the keyway and shoulder are both in the beam. Truck frame welds are scanned from both sides of the weld where access allows, because a flaw that is poorly oriented from one side often shows from the other.
  • Interpretation. Geometry reflectors such as keyways, weld roots and plate edges are known and marked on the sketch before scanning begins, so a true flaw is not confused with a legitimate echo.

What UT finds on mining equipment and what it misses

Method choice for common mining components
ComponentUT is the right choice whenAnother method is quicker when
Mill shell and trunnionYou need remaining wall or a buried flaw under a liner or flangeA surface crack at a weld toe is already suspected (use MT)
Haul truck frame weldThe crack may start below the surface or the weld is thickThe weld toe is clean and open to view (MT or PT)
Crusher or pulley shaftFatigue cracks grow from a keyway or shoulder into the bodyThe shaft is in a shop and the whole surface is accessible (MT)
Manganese steel liner or toothThickness onlySurface cracking, since the alloy is not magnetic (PT)

UT does not size every defect exactly. Very rough surfaces, coarse cast grain and thin paint-over-rust layers reduce what an operator can reliably say, and a crack that runs parallel to the sound beam may not return an echo. We tell you at quote stage when the geometry or the material will limit the examination. We do not perform radiography in the United States, and the specialist techniques some mines ask about are outside the scope of this page. If a component needs a method we do not offer, we say so rather than stretch UT to cover it.

Planning a mine job: access, training and conditions

Before any technician walks onto a mine, the operator must be satisfied about training and hazards. For contractors, that normally means site-specific hazard training under 30 CFR Part 46 for surface non-coal operations or Part 48 for underground and larger surface mines, arranged with the mine before arrival. Send us the name of the safety contact and the training the mine requires, and we will complete it before mobilizing. Expect to supply or approve personal protective equipment and any gas detectors, confined space permits for mill interiors and chutes, lock-out of rotating equipment, and escorts through haul roads.

Mill relines and truck rebuilds are the natural windows for UT, because shell, trunnion and frame surfaces are exposed and the equipment is already locked out. We can also work on running conveyors and idle trucks if the site approves. Remote sites bring practical issues: travel time, accommodation, weather, and sometimes no cell coverage, so we agree reporting arrangements in advance. We do not promise arrival times; we agree dates with the planner.

What the report contains

The report is built so a maintenance planner or an engineer can act on it without calling us. It lists the component identification and location, the procedure number and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block used, the calibration check results, and the technician's name and certification level. For thickness work it provides the grid or CML locations, each reading and the minimum found, with a sketch and photographs. For weld or shaft work it shows each indication with position, length, amplitude and depth, and states accept or reject against the named criteria. The Level III reviews and signs before release. If you want a general view of the method first, read the ultrasonic testing guide, or see the national UT page.

Castings and forgings such as bucket adapters, pins, gear blanks and crusher mainshaft forgings follow their own acceptance rules, and the separate page on ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings covers that work in more detail.

What to send for a quote

  • A list of components with drawings, weld maps or photographs, and the equipment model and serial number where the maker publishes inspection intervals.
  • Material and nominal thickness, and the coating or liner on each surface.
  • The code, specification or maker procedure that sets acceptance.
  • Access: scaffolds, lifts, confined spaces, working at height, and who provides them.
  • Site address, MSHA training required, escorts, permits and the shutdown window.
  • Whether you want thickness mapping only, crack detection, or both.

Training your own mine technicians

Many mines would rather have their own people take thickness readings between outside visits. Atlantis trains those technicians through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with practice on the ultrasonic testing simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so the mine's written practice governs; we can help build one through written practice development. The mine's own Level III can approve its procedures, or we can provide an outside ASNT Level III for that.

Other pages worth reading before you request a quote: pressure vessel inspection services for process vessels in the plant, and NDT technical procedure development for custom procedures on large equipment. Our quality system is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Can UT inspect a grinding mill shell without taking it apart?
faq.a: Yes for the shell plate and welds, because the transducer works from the outside surface. Liners and rubber must be removed or avoided where the sound has to pass, so the scope depends on whether the mill is relined at the time. We measure remaining thickness and look for weld cracking at heads, trunnion flanges and girth gear mounts.

faq.q: Does MSHA require ultrasonic testing of haul trucks?
faq.a: MSHA's 30 CFR Parts 56, 57, 75 and 77 require equipment to be kept in safe operating condition, but they do not prescribe UT. The decision to inspect comes from the maker's schedule, the mine's maintenance plan, or an incident. Your safety manager decides the scope; we perform it and report against the criteria you specify.

faq.q: How do you handle the mine's site training requirements?
faq.a: The mine tells us whether it needs site training under 30 CFR Part 46 or Part 48 and who delivers it. We complete it for each technician before mobilizing, so crews are not waiting at the gate. Send the contact and any badging forms with your inquiry.

faq.q: Can you test crusher shafts while they are still in the machine?
faq.a: Often, if the end face or a section of the diameter is accessible. Straight-beam and angle-beam scans from those positions detect fatigue cracks growing from keyways and shoulders. If a shaft is pulled to the shop, more of the surface is open and we can add magnetic particle testing for surface cracks.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic thickness testing accurate through paint and rubber?
faq.a: Paint is usually accepted by the measurement standard when the instrument is set up on a painted reference, but thick coatings and rubber add error and sometimes block the signal. We remove or avoid them where the quote or procedure calls for it, and the report records what was on the surface.

faq.q: Can UT find cracks in manganese steel liners and teeth?
faq.a: It reads thickness on them, but coarse grain scatters sound and limits crack detection. Because austenitic manganese steel is not magnetic, penetrant testing is the usual method for surface cracks on those parts. We recommend the right method at quote stage.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote UT on a truck or boom?
faq.a: Send the equipment model, drawings or weld maps if you have them, photographs of the areas of concern, the criteria that apply, and the site address with access and training requirements. A short list of components with locations is enough to start. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is rejected?
faq.a: The acceptance criteria belong to you, the equipment maker or the engineer of record, and our report compares each indication against them. We report what is there and the result against the named code. Repair, monitor or retire decisions remain with the owner or the engineer.

faq.q: Do you perform radiography on mining equipment?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because it is licensed work under federal or state radiation rules. Where a project needs it, the owner hires a licensed contractor. We can review radiographs and procedures as an ASNT Level III service, and our UT can often serve as the volumetric method.
